subject: physics

items.q: A rubber band is held by a clamp at one end while a student pulls the other end, and the band stretches. Which statement describes the forces that stretch the band?
items.correct: Two forces act on the band, pulling its two ends in opposite directions.
items.misconception: One pulling force acts on the band, along the line of the band.
items.why: In everyday language you pull a spring with one hand and it stretches, so the second force, supplied by whatever holds the other end, is never noticed. If a single force acted there would be a resultant force and the stationary object would accelerate away instead of changing shape. The clamp, hand or bench at the other end always supplies a second force.
items.random_wrong: Two forces act on the band, both pulling it towards the clamp.

items.q: A car is parked on level ground and the springs in its suspension are squashed. Which pair of forces compresses one of these springs?
items.correct: The car body pushes down on the spring and the axle pushes up on it.
items.misconception: The weight of the car is the only force acting on the spring.
items.why: The weight is the force the student adds and can see, while the upward pull of the stand on the top of the spring is invisible and easy to ignore. The stand supplies an equal upward force on the top of the spring. Two forces act in opposite directions, which is why the spring stretches instead of accelerating downwards.
items.random_wrong: The car body and the axle both push down on the spring from above it.

items.q: Why must more than one force be applied to a stationary object in order to change its shape?
items.correct: A single force would leave a resultant force, so the object would accelerate.
items.misconception: A single force is never large enough on its own to change the shape of an object.
items.why: In everyday language you pull a spring with one hand and it stretches, so the second force, supplied by whatever holds the other end, is never noticed. If a single force acted there would be a resultant force and the stationary object would accelerate away instead of changing shape. The clamp, hand or bench at the other end always supplies a second force.
items.random_wrong: Forces always occur in pairs, so a second force appears without being applied.

items.q: Which statement describes elastic deformation?
items.correct: The object returns to its original shape once the forces are removed.
items.misconception: The object keeps part of its extra length after the forces are removed.
items.why: The two terms are learnt as a pair and the labels are attached to the wrong behaviour, especially as every deformation involves a change of shape. The test is what happens after the force is removed: returning to the original shape is elastic deformation; staying deformed is inelastic deformation.
items.random_wrong: The object is made of rubber, so it stretches much further than metal does.

items.q: A steel spring is stretched by a very large force. When the force is removed the spring is longer than it was at the start. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: It has been inelastically deformed, so it has not returned to its original shape.
items.misconception: It has been elastically deformed, because its shape changed while pulled.
items.why: The two terms are learnt as a pair and the labels are attached to the wrong behaviour, especially as every deformation involves a change of shape. The test is what happens after the force is removed: returning to the original shape is elastic deformation; staying deformed is inelastic deformation.
items.random_wrong: It cannot have deformed elastically, since steel is not a stretchy material.

items.q: A spring is loaded with weights, staying below its limit of proportionality. Which statement about the force and the extension is correct?
items.correct: The extension is directly proportional to the force applied to the spring.
items.misconception: The extension is directly proportional to the total length of the spring used.
items.why: The word 'extension' is heard as 'the extended length', and the stretched length is the number the ruler shows. Extension is the increase in length: stretched length - original length. Here that is 8.5 - 5.0 = 3.5 cm, which is 0.035 m.
items.random_wrong: The force is proportional to the extension whatever the load size.

items.q: What does the limit of proportionality of a spring tell you?
items.correct: The largest force for which extension stays proportional to force.
items.misconception: The force at which the spring finally snaps and can carry no more load.
items.why: 'Limit' is read as the end of the spring's useful life, so it is confused with the breaking point. At the limit of proportionality the graph stops being a straight line. The spring can still be stretched further; it just extends by more per newton, and it may become inelastically deformed.
items.random_wrong: The force beyond which the spring will not return to its original length.

items.q: A spring has a spring constant of 120 N/m and is stretched by 25 cm, which is below its limit of proportionality. Using force = spring constant × extension, what is the force applied to the spring?
items.why: The centimetre figure is used straight from the table, because the equation does not look as though it cares about units. The extension must be in metres: 12 cm = 0.12 m, so k = 6.0 / 0.12 = 50 N/m.

items.q: Which statement about the quantities in the equation F = k e is correct?
items.correct: The spring constant, k, is measured in newtons per metre, written N/m.
items.misconception: The spring constant, k, is measured in newtons, N, as a force is.
items.why: Every symbol in F = k e is associated with the force being calculated, and N is the unit that comes to mind for anything to do with springs. The spring constant is a force per unit extension, so its unit is newtons per metre, N/m. Only F is in newtons.
items.random_wrong: The extension, e, is measured in centimetres, cm, in this equation.

items.q: A force of 6.0 N stretches a spring by 12 cm. The limit of proportionality has not been exceeded. What is the spring constant of this spring?
items.correct: 50 N/m
items.why: The centimetre figure is used straight from the table, because the equation does not look as though it cares about units. The extension must be in metres: 12 cm = 0.12 m, so k = 6.0 / 0.12 = 50 N/m.

items.q: Spring A has a spring constant of 30 N/m and spring B has a spring constant of 90 N/m. The same force is applied to each spring. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: Spring B extends less, because a larger spring constant means a stiffer spring.
items.misconception: Spring B extends more, because a larger spring constant means more stretch.
items.why: A large number is read as 'more of everything', so a large k is assumed to mean a large stretch. Rearranging F = k e gives e = F / k, so for the same force a larger spring constant gives a smaller extension. A large k means a stiff spring that is hard to stretch.
items.random_wrong: Both springs extend by exactly the same amount, because the same force is applied.

items.q: A spring is squashed rather than stretched. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: F = k e still applies, with e as the compression of the spring.
items.misconception: A different equation is needed, because F = k e only covers stretching.
items.why: The equation is always met in the context of stretching, so compression is assumed to be a separate case with its own rule. The specification states that the relationship also applies to compression, with e standing for the compression of the object.
items.random_wrong: No energy is stored, because energy is only stored by stretching a spring.

items.q: A spring is stretched by a force and is not inelastically deformed. How does the elastic potential energy stored compare with the work done on the spring?
items.correct: The energy stored is equal to the work done on the spring by the force.
items.misconception: The energy stored is slightly less, because some energy is wasted.
items.why: The rule that energy transfers are never fully useful is applied here, even though the specification states the two are equal for a spring that is not inelastically deformed. Provided the spring is not inelastically deformed, the work done on the spring and the elastic potential energy stored in it are equal.
items.random_wrong: The energy stored is larger, because the spring pulls back as well.

items.q: A spring is stretched so far that it is inelastically deformed. Which statement about the work done on the spring is correct?
items.correct: The work done is greater than the elastic potential energy stored in it.
items.misconception: The work done is still exactly equal to the elastic potential energy stored.
items.why: The statement 'work done = energy stored' is remembered without the condition attached to it in the specification. The equality holds only if the spring is not inelastically deformed. When it is permanently deformed, some of the work done is transferred to the thermal energy store instead of being stored elastically.
items.random_wrong: The work done is less than the energy stored, as the spring is longer.

items.q: A force-extension graph for a spring is a straight line through the origin up to 8 N, and curves above 8 N. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: The relationship is linear up to 8 N and non-linear above 8 N.
items.misconception: The relationship is non-linear throughout, because the graph is not straight.
items.why: Students are told to look for anomalies and to expect a straight line, so any departure from a straight line is read as experimental error. A smooth, repeatable curve at the top of the graph is real physics: beyond the limit of proportionality the extension is no longer proportional to the force. An anomaly is a single point off an otherwise smooth trend.
items.random_wrong: The curved part shows the spring becoming stiffer as the load increases.

items.q: A spring with a spring constant of 2000 N/m is stretched by 8.0 cm, below its limit of proportionality. Using elastic potential energy = 0.5 × spring constant × (extension)^2, how much energy is stored?
items.why: The centimetre figure is used straight from the table, because the equation does not look as though it cares about units. The extension must be in metres: 12 cm = 0.12 m, so k = 6.0 / 0.12 = 50 N/m.

items.q: The extension of a spring is doubled, and the spring stays below its limit of proportionality. What happens to the elastic potential energy stored in it?
items.correct: It becomes four times as large, because the extension is squared.
items.misconception: It doubles, because the energy is proportional to the extension.
items.why: Proportional reasoning learnt from F = k e is carried over to the energy equation without noticing the extension is squared. E_e = 1/2 k e^2, so the energy depends on the square of the extension. Doubling e multiplies the stored energy by 2^2 = 4.
items.random_wrong: It stays the same, because the spring constant has not changed.

items.q: A spring with a spring constant of 800 N/m is compressed by 3.0 cm and then released, pushing a trolley along a smooth bench. Which statement describes the main energy transfer?
items.correct: The elastic potential energy store of the spring empties to the kinetic store.
items.misconception: The kinetic energy store of the trolley fills up the elastic store of the spring.
items.why: Storing energy is pictured as 'pulling something back', so squashing does not look like a way of storing energy. A force that compresses a spring does work on it, so elastic potential energy is stored, and it is released when the spring pushes back.
items.random_wrong: No energy is transferred, because a compressed spring stores no energy.

items.q: In an investigation of force and extension, a student records: 1.0 N, 2.0 cm; 2.0 N, 4.0 cm; 3.0 N, 6.0 cm; 4.0 N, 8.0 cm; 5.0 N, 12.0 cm. Which conclusion is best supported?
items.correct: The first four points give k = 50 N/m, and the last point is off the line.
items.misconception: All five points fit a straight line, so k is 50 N/m for the spring.
items.why: Students are told to look for anomalies and to expect a straight line, so any departure from a straight line is read as experimental error. A smooth, repeatable curve at the top of the graph is real physics: beyond the limit of proportionality the extension is no longer proportional to the force. An anomaly is a single point off an otherwise smooth trend.
items.random_wrong: The spring constant is 0.42 N/m, taken from the last pair of readings.

items.q: In required practical activity 6, a spring hangs from a clamp stand and weights are added one at a time. Which method gives the most reliable value for the extension?
items.correct: Measure the loaded length at eye level and subtract the original length.
items.misconception: Take the spring off the stand after each weight and measure it flat on the bench.
items.why: Measuring something lying on the bench feels easier and more accurate than measuring something hanging in mid-air. The spring must be measured while the load is still on it, because removing the load lets the spring return to its original length and the extension is lost.
items.random_wrong: Read the ruler from wherever you are sitting, since a scale reading cannot change.

items.q: Two forces act on a rubber band. Will they always stretch it?
items.correct: Only if they act in opposite directions, pulling the two ends apart.
items.misconception: Any two forces will stretch it, because more than one force is acting.
items.why: The rule is memorised as a count of forces, so the direction of each force is never checked. Two forces acting the same way would give a resultant force and move the band. To stretch it the forces must pull the ends in opposite directions; to compress it they must push the ends together.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can a steel spring be deformed elastically?
items.correct: Yes – elastic deformation is about behaviour, not about the material.
items.misconception: No – elastic means rubbery, so only rubber-like materials are elastic.
items.why: The everyday word 'elastic' names a material (an elastic band), so the physics meaning gets attached to soft, stretchy substances. In physics, elastic deformation means the object returns to its original shape when the force is removed. A steel spring does exactly that, so it is behaving elastically.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What does inelastic deformation mean?
items.correct: The object does not return to its original shape when the force is removed.
items.misconception: The object snaps or breaks into pieces.
items.why: 'Inelastic' sounds like failure, and the most memorable way a stretched object can fail is by breaking. Inelastic deformation means a permanent change of shape: the object stays longer or bent after the force is removed. It is still in one piece.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does F = k e work for any force applied to a spring?
items.correct: Only up to the limit of proportionality.
items.misconception: Yes – it is the spring equation, so it works for every load.
items.why: Equations are learnt as unconditional rules, and the proviso in the specification is easy to drop when recalling the formula. Beyond the limit of proportionality extension is no longer directly proportional to force, the graph curves, and F = k e no longer gives the right answer.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How do you find the spring constant from a force-extension graph?
items.correct: It is the gradient of the straight-line part with force on the vertical axis.
items.misconception: It is the gradient whichever quantity is plotted on which axis.
items.why: 'Gradient = spring constant' is memorised as a rule without the condition about which quantity goes on which axis. With force on the vertical axis and extension on the horizontal axis the gradient is F / e = k. If the axes are swapped the gradient is e / F, which is 1 / k.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Beyond the limit of proportionality the graph bends towards the extension axis. What does this mean?
items.correct: The spring extends more for each extra newton than it did before.
items.misconception: The spring is getting stiffer as the load grows.
items.why: Any bend in a graph is read as 'harder', and a stretched spring feels tighter, so 'stiffer' seems the natural description. The graph bending away from the straight line means each extra newton now produces a larger extension than before, so the spring is easier, not harder, to stretch further.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What does the area under a linear force-extension graph give?
items.correct: The work done, which equals the elastic potential energy stored.
items.misconception: The spring constant of the spring.
items.why: Gradient and area are both 'things you get off a graph', and the spring constant is the quantity most associated with this graph. The gradient gives the spring constant; the area under the line gives the work done on the spring, which equals the energy stored.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How is the energy stored in a stretched spring calculated?
items.correct: Using E_e = 1/2 k e^2.
items.misconception: By multiplying the force by the extension.
items.why: Work done = force × distance is applied directly, ignoring that the force grows from zero as the spring stretches. The force increases from zero as the spring stretches, so the energy stored is 1/2 k e^2, which is half of F e for a linear spring.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A spring is held stretched by a steady force. Has work been done on it?
items.correct: Yes – work was done while it was being stretched.
items.misconception: No – the spring is not moving, so no work has been done.
items.why: Work is linked to visible motion, and a stretched spring held still looks like a situation with no movement at all. Work is done while the spring is being extended, because the applied force moves through a distance. That work is stored as elastic potential energy.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How should the ruler be read when measuring the length of a loaded spring?
items.correct: At eye level, with the ruler vertical next to the spring.
items.misconception: From wherever you happen to be sitting; eye position cannot change a ruler reading.
items.why: The scale looks like a fixed, objective thing, so the idea that the reading depends on the line of sight is not obvious. Reading from above or below causes a parallax error. The ruler should be vertical, clamped next to the spring, and read at eye level.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why must a second force be applied to deform a stationary object?
items.correct: Because a single force would leave a resultant force and the object would accelerate.
items.misconception: Because forces come in pairs anyway, so a second force appears by itself.
items.why: Newton's third law is remembered as 'forces come in pairs', which is then used to explain away the need to apply a second force. The two forces that deform an object act on the same object and must both be applied to it. A third-law pair acts on two different objects and could not squash or stretch anything on its own.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Two springs are given the same force. Do they extend by the same amount?
items.correct: No – the extension also depends on the spring constant.
items.misconception: Yes – the same force always produces the same extension.
items.why: Force is treated as the only thing that matters, so the stiffness of the spring drops out of the reasoning. From e = F / k, the same force gives a smaller extension in a spring with a larger spring constant.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A spring has k = 120 N/m and an extension of 0.25 m. How is the force found?
items.correct: By multiplying: F = k e = 120 × 0.25.
items.misconception: By dividing the two numbers, because that is what you do with an equation like this.
items.why: F = k e is remembered as a formula triangle and the division is carried out the wrong way round, especially when one number is smaller than one. F is already the subject of the equation, so k and e are multiplied. Division is used only when F is known and k or e is being found.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification; section 4.5.3 Forces and elasticity
